tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

type.description: What kind of feedback this is.

title.description: Short, specific one-line summary of the issue.

details.description: Labeled bullets, in order: **What happened:** (observed vs. expected, exact error text if short); **What the user said:** (quoted, or "User didn't comment; observed by the model."); **Repro:** (minimal steps); **Evidence:** (request IDs, timestamps, paths, versions; omit if none); optionally a final **Cause:** only if verified in-session. One to three lines per bullet. No narrative paragraphs, no speculation, no secrets.

area.description: Optional short tag naming the part of Claude Code this is about (e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing"). Leave blank if unclear.

failure_mode.description: When the report is about MODEL BEHAVIOR (not a product bug), the closest failure mode, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value. Omit only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.

task_category.description: What kind of task the session was doing when the issue occurred, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

Writes a file to the local filesystem, overwriting if one exists.

When to use: creating a new file, or fully replacing one you've already Read. Overwriting an existing file you haven't Read will fail. For partial changes, use Edit instead.

Rod, a quick update. I've read the port rules and Pong's source, and Linear has no ticket for it. AGENTS.md says to ask before starting work without one, so I'm stopping to ask.

**How hard is it? Moderate, with one big risk (speed).**

- **The code to copy:** `pong.c` is 1,108 lines of game logic. It draws everything through `analogtv`, xscreensaver's NTSC TV emulator. That means copying `analogtv.c` (2,459 lines) and `analogtv.h` unmodified.
- **What isn't ported yet:** nothing in the firmware uses `analogtv` today. Pong and `analogtv.c` need these shim gaps filled:
  - **Pointer and cursor calls:** `XGrabPointer`, `XUngrabPointer`, `XWarpPointer`, `XCreatePixmapCursor` and `XDefineCursor`.
  - **Screen and event names:** `XHeightMMOfScreen`, `XHeightOfScreen`, the event masks and `X11/keysym.h`.

  Most of these can be no-ops. The existing `xshm.h`, `thread_util.h` and `ximage.c` already cover the rest.
- **Memory:** `analogtv` holds a signal buffer of about 262 × 912 floats, roughly 1 MB. That goes in PSRAM, which has room.
- **Speed (the real risk):** each frame it synthesises and filters about 240,000 NTSC samples. It also mixes `double` and `float` maths, and the S3 has a single-precision FPU only. It then writes a window-sized image, and a full-frame PSRAM write costs about 25 ms. My guess, not a measurement, is 3–8 fps as copied.
- **Likely fixes:** a single-precision wrapper, a lower `ANALOGTV_SCALE`, no noise or ghosting, and a smaller render size via `lowrez_put.h`. If it stays under about 8 fps, the honest answer may be to drop it, as with Boing.

**Can I file a Linear ticket on ARS for the Pong port (labels `stopwatch-screensaver` plus a Work Type, a priority, status In Progress) and start on `feature/ARS-NN-pong`?** The first step would be the failing registry test, then the shim gaps, then a host dump to measure the step time.

# Linear tracking

Moved verbatim from AGENTS.md.

## Filing issues

- Every issue gets the `stopwatch-screensaver` label (in the `Repo` group) and exactly
  one label from the `Work Type` group. The group is single-select, so
  pick the one that fits best (see below).
- Always set a priority (Urgent, High, Medium, Low). Never leave it at
  "No priority".
- Link the draft trail or spec section if one exists. Copy the body from
  `entire trail show N --json`; `entire trail list --json` returns empty
  bodies.

## Choosing a Work Type

| Label         | Use it for                                       |
| ------------- | ------------------------------------------------ |
| `Bug`         | Fixing something that isn't operating correctly. |
| `Feature`     | Adding new functionality to the app.             |
| `Enhancement` | Improving existing functionality.                |
| `Performance` | Improving the performance of code.               |
| `Chore`       | Maintenance, tooling and documentation work.     |

Several of these can fit one ticket. Decide by asking these in order and
taking the first yes:

1. Does the app do something other than what was intended? `Bug`, even if
   the symptom is slowness or the fix is a refactor.
1. Is the behaviour right, but too slow or heavy, and is speed or
   resource use the point of the work? `Performance`.
1. Does it give the user a capability they did not have? `Feature`.
1. Does it make a capability they already have better? `Enhancement`.
1. Does it change nothing a user would notice? `Chore`.

A ticket that bundles small, unrelated tidy-ups takes `Chore`. If the
bundle is mostly one other type, either split it or use that type.
Refactors, test additions, dependency bumps, build scripts, CI and
documentation are `Chore` unless they fix a defect.

## Status names

Use these exactly as Linear spells them: `Backlog`, `Todo`,
`In Progress`, `In Review`, `Done`, `Canceled`, `Duplicate`.

# Working in a git worktree

Moved verbatim from AGENTS.md.

- In a git worktree the ignored `vendor/`, `.venv/` and `.platformio/` are
  missing. Symlink them from the main checkout. `.gitignore`'s trailing slashes
  don't match symlinks, so they would show as untracked, but the shared
  `.git/info/exclude` already lists the three names. That file is shared by
  every worktree: ask Rod before adding to it.
  The harness refuses `source tools/env.sh` and a computed `PATH` there: run
  `PLATFORMIO_CORE_DIR=<worktree>/.platformio ../.venv/bin/pio ...` instead,
  and keep commands plain (no scripts, loops, `$VAR` in a command or `&&`
  chains with a computed path). A worktree an agent works in (`isolation:
  "worktree"`) starts from `origin/main`, not from your branch, and has no
  vendor or toolchain until you link them.
  It also refuses heredocs, `git -C` and `cd` into another worktree: use the
  Edit and Write tools. It refuses `git ... | tar` and `cd <dir> && git ...`
  too: use `git archive -o f.tar <sha>` then `tar -x -f f.tar -C <dir>`, and run
  git from the worktree root. A background shell starts there as well, so use
  `pio test -d <abs>/firmware` with absolute paths. Parallel calls can race
  (a `uv run` in the root disturbed `.venv` while `pio` ran:
  "../.venv/bin/pio: no such file"), so run
  `uv` and `pio` one at a time. To fast-forward `main` or remove the worktree,
  leave it first with `ExitWorktree keep`. If no checkout has `main` out,
  `git fetch origin main:main` fast-forwards it from anywhere.
  Before `ExitWorktree remove` on a merged branch, check
  `git merge-base --is-ancestor <tip> origin/main`; the tool's "discarded N
  commits" count ignores merges. `.platformio`, `.venv` and `vendor` there are
  symlinks, so removal leaves the real ones alone. After a merge,
  `ExitWorktree keep` names a branch (`worktree-<name>`) that may not exist:
  remove the worktree with `git worktree remove --force <path>` and delete the
  real branch, as separate commands, because a failed `&&` link skips the rest
  silently. Check `git worktree list` afterwards. `git worktree remove --force`
  fails on a worktree this session's harness locked ("cannot remove a locked
  working tree, lock reason: claude session"): once the tip is an ancestor of
  `origin/main`, `ExitWorktree remove` with `discard_changes: true` works, and
  its "discarded N commits" are the merged ones. In a session resumed from a
  summary, `ExitWorktree` can be a no-op ("no active EnterWorktree session"):
  remove the worktree with `git worktree remove --force <path>` from the main
  checkout instead. To delete the merged branch
  you are standing on, `git switch --detach origin/main` in the worktree first.
  The shell's directory resets after each command and after `ExitWorktree`, so
  use absolute paths (`../.venv/bin/pio` failed from the wrong place and the run
  looked like a test failure). A loop over several mutations is refused as a
  command: write it as a script in the scratchpad that edits the file, runs
  `pio test` through `subprocess` and restores the file in `finally`, then run
  it with `python3 -I`.
  Stopping such a script (TaskStop) kills it before `finally` runs: check
  `git diff` afterwards and restore the file by hand.
  Also refused: a heredoc (use the Write tool for a scratchpad script), `$(...)`
  inside a git command, and the quoted `PLATFORMIO_BUILD_FLAGS` above combined
  with a redirect or `NO_COLOR=1`. Flashing worked as
  `PLATFORMIO_CORE_DIR=<wt>/.platformio PLATFORMIO_BUILD_FLAGS="..."
  .venv/bin/pio run -d firmware -e stopwatch -t upload` with no redirect: the
  540 KB of output lands in a tool-results file, so grep that for "Hash of data
  verified". Edit and Write refuse the main checkout's path while you are in a
  worktree. `pio test -f test_x` runs the whole suite (`test_hacks` takes 3
  minutes, the full native run 7), and a failing summary reads "2 failed, 101
  succeeded": match `[FAILED]` or the return code, not "succeeded".
- `uv run ty check` (the pre-commit `ty` hook) fails in a worktree with
  "Failed to spawn: ty": the shared `.venv` has no `ty`. Run
  `uvx ty check --python .venv` instead (it passes on a clean tree), then
  commit with `SKIP=ty git commit ...`, and say in the PR that the hook was
  skipped. `ruff-format` rewrites a file and aborts the commit when a line is
  too long: restage the file and commit again.
- Also refused in a worktree session: a shell variable used as a program's
  argument (`S=...; prog $S/x`), a `for` loop that runs `uv` or `pio`, and
  `entire trail finding resolve -m "..."` text containing `*` or backticks.
  Spell out absolute paths, run one command per call, and keep `-m` text to
  plain words.

content.content:
# Testing gotchas

Moved verbatim from AGENTS.md.

- A mutant that sends every case to the fallback path is equivalent, not a
  gap: it passes because the old arithmetic runs. Change the rounding without
  forcing the fallback. A guard justified by an error bound (a limit, a
  reseed interval) can survive a mutant when failures are one in millions:
  say so in the PR rather than hunting for a test.
- Host tests cannot prove the 16 KB loop stack: `ulimit -s` sees only the
  shallow first level of a random recursion, and AddressSanitizer inflates
  frames. Use `stack_used_by` in `test_hacks.c` (a painted pthread stack) and,
  on the device, `uxTaskGetStackHighWaterMark` in the stats line (temporary).
- `pio test` runs every registered hack for 3000 frames under ASan (about 15 s);
  a hack that is slow on the host slows the whole suite.
- Host leak tests: LeakSanitizer does not run on macOS, so compare
  `__sanitizer_get_current_allocated_bytes()`
  (`<sanitizer/allocator_interface.h>`) before and after many restarts, as in
  `test_hacks.c`.
  Take both readings at rest (after `runner_destroy`): a reading while a hack
  runs counts random-sized live state (Loop swings about 1 MB by mode), so
  the verdict depends on test order.
- AddressSanitizer cannot see an index past an array inside a struct
  (`pp->Cells[x][25][z]`). Build with `-fsanitize=address,array-bounds
  -fno-sanitize-recover=all` to check such a claim, and prove first that it
  fires on a small probe.
- `pio test` hides `printf` and stderr from tests. To see two values, assert
  `TEST_ASSERT_EQUAL_UINT64(a, b)` temporarily: the failure line prints both.
- To survey many hacks on the host (flushes per frame, say), add a temporary
  test that `fopen`s `getenv("SURVEY_OUT")` and writes lines; run
  `SURVEY_OUT=<file> pio test -e native -f test_push_present`, then
  `git checkout` the test. `PLATFORMIO_BUILD_FLAGS=-D...` varies a constant.
- `test_frames_of_every_hack_but_maze_match_main` stops at the first moved
  hash, so the others hide behind it. To list all of them, temporarily append
  `name idx got=0x...` to a buffer and `TEST_FAIL_MESSAGE` it (`TEST_MESSAGE`
  is hidden too), then `git checkout` the file. The failure prints decimal;
  `python3 -c "print(hex(N))"` gives the `kBaseline` form.
- A hack allocates its state on the first `runner_step`, not at
  `runner_start`: a test that reads a hack's globals (`pacman_games[0]`)
  before one step gets NULL, and ASan reports a SEGV on a write near address 0.
- A mutation that keeps the file's size (`if (0)` to `if (1)`), restored in
  the same second, leaves a stale `.pyc` that the next `pytest` run loads:
  delete `tools/__pycache__/<module>*.pyc` after a mutation script, then
  rerun before trusting a failure.
- On a busy Mac (load average over 10) the suite can look hung. Before
  killing it, `sample $(pgrep -f .pio/build/native/program) 3` shows where it
  is: it was in Unknown Pleasures, slow but moving.
- Mutation-checking wrap-around code: a mutation that just reorders unsigned
  arithmetic can be equivalent and survive. Use `int64_t` to break it for real.
- A guard condition already implied elsewhere (`color_valid &&` where an
  invalid side is fully cleared anyway) leaves an equivalent mutant that
  survives: drop it, so every part of the guard can be killed.
- After a mutation check, `grep` that the change applied: a `sed` that matches
  nothing leaves the tests green and proves nothing. Restore the file and
  confirm with `cmp` or `git diff`.
- Restoring after a mutation: commit (or copy) the real change first.
  `git checkout <file>` reverts everything uncommitted in it, fix included.
  The scratchpad mutation script restores from its in-memory original.
- Mutating a regex or any pattern with backslashes: write the mutation as a
  scratchpad script (as the loop-of-mutations gotcha says) and `assert old in
  text` first. Shell quoting doubles the backslashes, nothing changes, and the
  passing run looks like a surviving mutant.
- Unity marks a failing test `[FAILED]` at the end of its line, not `:FAIL`. A
  mutation script that greps for `:FAIL` reports every mutant as surviving.
- A mutant can die by crash, not assertion: an ASan abort ends the run with
  "20 test cases: 19 succeeded" (fewer cases than usual, no `[FAILED]`). Read
  the summary line and treat anything but the full passing count as killed.
- To test code inside a wrapped hack (a `static inline` blend, say), give the
  test its own dir and `#define <name>_hack <name>_hack_under_test` before
  `#include "hacks/<name>_direct.c"`: the wrapper exports only that one symbol,
  so it links beside the registered copy. See `test_interaggregate_blend`.
- `pio test -e native -f test_<dir>` runs one suite (the xshim and
  single-hack tests take about a second); `test_hacks` alone takes about
  2m20s and the whole `pio test -e native` about 5 minutes.
- `pio test` hides which test crashed and AddressSanitizer's report: after a
  failure, run `.pio/build/native/program` from `firmware/` for the per-test
  PASS/FAIL lines and the ASan stack.
- A mutation script must run the unmutated tree first and stop if it fails:
  a test that fails for another reason (Phosphor's included the paged poem
  header while the wrapper used the scrolling one) makes every mutant look

# Testing gotchas

Moved verbatim from AGENTS.md.

- A mutant that sends every case to the fallback path is equivalent, not a
  gap: it passes because the old arithmetic runs. Change the rounding without
  forcing the fallback. A guard justified by an error bound (a limit, a
  reseed interval) can survive a mutant when failures are one in millions:
  say so in the PR rather than hunting for a test.
- Host tests cannot prove the 16 KB loop stack: `ulimit -s` sees only the
  shallow first level of a random recursion, and AddressSanitizer inflates
  frames. Use `stack_used_by` in `test_hacks.c` (a painted pthread stack) and,
  on the device, `uxTaskGetStackHighWaterMark` in the stats line (temporary).
- `pio test` runs every registered hack for 3000 frames under ASan (about 15 s);
  a hack that is slow on the host slows the whole suite.
- Host leak tests: LeakSanitizer does not run on macOS, so compare
  `__sanitizer_get_current_allocated_bytes()`
  (`<sanitizer/allocator_interface.h>`) before and after many restarts, as in
  `test_hacks.c`.
  Take both readings at rest (after `runner_destroy`): a reading while a hack
  runs counts random-sized live state (Loop swings about 1 MB by mode), so
  the verdict depends on test order.
- AddressSanitizer cannot see an index past an array inside a struct
  (`pp->Cells[x][25][z]`). Build with `-fsanitize=address,array-bounds
  -fno-sanitize-recover=all` to check such a claim, and prove first that it
  fires on a small probe.
- `pio test` hides `printf` and stderr from tests. To see two values, assert
  `TEST_ASSERT_EQUAL_UINT64(a, b)` temporarily: the failure line prints both.
- To survey many hacks on the host (flushes per frame, say), add a temporary
  test that `fopen`s `getenv("SURVEY_OUT")` and writes lines; run
  `SURVEY_OUT=<file> pio test -e native -f test_push_present`, then
  `git checkout` the test. `PLATFORMIO_BUILD_FLAGS=-D...` varies a constant.
- `test_frames_of_every_hack_but_maze_match_main` stops at the first moved
  hash, so the others hide behind it. To list all of them, temporarily append
  `name idx got=0x...` to a buffer and `TEST_FAIL_MESSAGE` it (`TEST_MESSAGE`
  is hidden too), then `git checkout` the file. The failure prints decimal;
  `python3 -c "print(hex(N))"` gives the `kBaseline` form.
- A hack allocates its state on the first `runner_step`, not at
  `runner_start`: a test that reads a hack's globals (`pacman_games[0]`)
  before one step gets NULL, and ASan reports a SEGV on a write near address 0.
- A mutation that keeps the file's size (`if (0)` to `if (1)`), restored in
  the same second, leaves a stale `.pyc` that the next `pytest` run loads:
  delete `tools/__pycache__/<module>*.pyc` after a mutation script, then
  rerun before trusting a failure.

  killing it, `sample $(pgrep -f .pio/build/native/program) 3` shows where it
  is: it was in Unknown Pleasures, slow but moving.
- Mutation-checking wrap-around code: a mutation that just reorders unsigned
  arithmetic can be equivalent and survive. Use `int64_t` to break it for real.
- A guard condition already implied elsewhere (`color_valid &&` where an
  invalid side is fully cleared anyway) leaves an equivalent mutant that
  survives: drop it, so every part of the guard can be killed.

- A mutation script must run the unmutated tree first and stop if it fails:
  a test that fails for another reason (Phosphor's included the paged poem
  header while the wrapper used the scrolling one) makes every mutant look
  killed. Print the baseline's result, not only the mutants'.

"""Mutation check for the Pong shim gaps and wrapper. Run with python3 -I."""

import subprocess
import sys
from pathlib import Path

WT = Path("/Users/rod/build/stopwatch-screensaver/.claude/worktrees/pong")
FW = WT / "firmware"
PIO = WT / ".venv" / "bin" / "pio"
ENV = {
    "PATH": "/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/sbin:/opt/homebrew/bin",
    "HOME": "/Users/rod",
    "PLATFORMIO_CORE_DIR": str(WT / ".platformio"),
    "NO_COLOR": "1",
}

MUTANTS = [
    ("wrapper: no swap of red", "firmware/src/hacks/pong_tv.c",
     "it->red_values[i] = px_swap((uint16_t)it->red_values[i]);",
     "it->red_values[i] = (uint16_t)it->red_values[i];", "test_pong_wrapper"),
    ("wrapper: no swap of green", "firmware/src/hacks/pong_tv.c",
     "it->green_values[i] = px_swap((uint16_t)it->green_values[i]);",
     "it->green_values[i] = (uint16_t)it->green_values[i];", "test_pong_wrapper"),
    ("wrapper: no swap of blue", "firmware/src/hacks/pong_tv.c",
     "it->blue_values[i] = px_swap((uint16_t)it->blue_values[i]);",
     "it->blue_values[i] = (uint16_t)it->blue_values[i];", "test_pong_wrapper"),
    ("wrapper: swap only when use_cmap", "firmware/src/hacks/pong_tv.c",
     "if (it && !it->use_cmap) {", "if (it && it->use_cmap) {", "test_pong_wrapper"),
    ("shim: screen height wrong", "firmware/src/x11shim/xshim.c",
     "return g_current_display ? g_current_display->canvas->h : 0;",
     "return g_current_display ? g_current_display->canvas->w + 1 : 0;", "test_xshim"),
    ("shim: panel height wrong", "firmware/src/x11shim/xshim.h",
     "#define XHeightMMOfScreen(screen) ((void)(screen), 44)",
     "#define XHeightMMOfScreen(screen) ((void)(screen), 45)", "test_xshim"),
    ("shim: grab fails", "firmware/src/x11shim/xshim.c",
     "(void)keyboard_mode, (void)confine_to, (void)cursor, (void)time;\n  return GrabSuccess;",
     "(void)keyboard_mode, (void)confine_to, (void)cursor, (void)time;\n  return 1;", "test_xshim"),
    ("shim: visual not true colour", "firmware/src/x11shim/xshm.c",
     "  return TrueColor;", "  return PseudoColor;", "test_xshim"),
    ("shim: red mask wrong", "firmware/src/x11shim/xshm.c",
     "*red_mask = 0xF800;", "*red_mask = 0x7C00;", "test_xshim"),
    ("shim: green mask wrong", "firmware/src/x11shim/xshm.c",
     "*green_mask = 0x07E0;", "*green_mask = 0x03E0;", "test_xshim"),
    ("shim: thread_malloc never fails but returns nothing", "firmware/src/x11shim/thread_util.c",
     "*ptr = malloc(size);", "*ptr = calloc(1, 1);", "test_xshim"),
    ("shim: XQueryColors does only the first", "firmware/src/x11shim/xshim.c",
     "for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) XQueryColor(dpy, cmap, &colors[i]);",
     "for (int i = 0; i < 1 && i < n; i++) XQueryColor(dpy, cmap, &colors[i]);", "test_xshim"),
    ("shim: format not recorded", "firmware/src/x11shim/ximage.c",
     "  im->format = format;\n", "", "test_xshim"),
    ("shim: XYPixmap refused", "firmware/src/x11shim/ximage.c",
     "(format == XYBitmap || format == XYPixmap) && depth == 1",
     "format == XYBitmap && depth == 1", "test_xshim"),
    ("shim: FocusChangeMask wrong", "firmware/src/x11shim/xshim.h",
     "#define FocusChangeMask (1L << 21)", "#define FocusChangeMask (1L << 20)", "test_xshim"),
]


def run(test: str) -> tuple[int, str]:
    p = subprocess.run(
        [str(PIO), "test", "-e", "native", "-f", test],
        cwd=FW, env=ENV, capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=900,
    )
    out = p.stdout + p.stderr
    summary = [l for l in out.splitlines() if "test cases" in l]
    return p.returncode, (summary[-1] if summary else "no summary")


def main() -> int:
    for t in ("test_pong_wrapper", "test_xshim"):
        rc, s = run(t)
        print(f"BASELINE {t}: rc={rc} {s}", flush=True)
        if rc != 0:
            print("baseline fails: stopping")
            return 1
    survived = []
    for name, rel, old, new, test in MUTANTS:
        path = WT / rel
        original = path.read_text()
        assert original.count(old) == 1, (name, original.count(old))
        try:
            path.write_text(original.replace(old, new))
            assert path.read_text() != original
            rc, s = run(test)
        finally:
            path.write_text(original)
        verdict = "killed" if rc != 0 else "SURVIVED"
        if rc == 0:
            survived.append(name)
        print(f"{verdict}: {name} ({test}: {s})", flush=True)
    print("survivors:", survived)
    return 0


sys.exit(main())

Rod, Pong is ported on the host and committed as WIP (789ec6b on `feature/ARS-59-pong`). I need your go-ahead to flash, because speed and stack can only be measured on the board.

**What's done and checked**
- **Source:** the copies of `pong.c`, `analogtv.c` and `analogtv.h` are byte-identical to upstream (`cmp`), and `check_notices.py` passes.
- **Build:** they build as one unit through `hacks/pong_tv.c`. The wrapper swaps analogtv's colour tables once, so pixels come out in canvas byte order with no per-pixel cost.
- **Shim gaps filled test-first:**
  - **Pointer, cursor and focus:** no-ops for `XGrabPointer`, `XWarpPointer`, `XDefineCursor` and friends.
  - **Visual and screen:** screen height, `visual_class`, and RGB565 masks.
  - **Memory and colours:** `thread_malloc`, `XQueryColors`, `XImage.format`, one-bit `XYPixmap` images, and a few compatibility headers.
- **Tests:**
  - **Mutation checks:** all 15 mutants were killed.
  - **`test_xshim`:** 314 of 314 pass.
  - **`test_hacks`:** 150 of 150 pass, including the leak test and the stop-before-first-frame test.
  - **Pong wrapper test:** 2 of 2 pass.
- **Builds:** the dump build and the device build both compile and link.
- **Frames:** I viewed frames at 200 and 1500 on the host. It's authentic Pong with scores, ball, paddles, NTSC noise and ghosting.

**Not yet established**
- **Speed:** the host step is 3.6 ms, which isn't a guide to the S3. My estimate is 5–8 fps, which is a guess.
- **Stack:** the line loop frame is 9,328 bytes and the filter's is 3,264 bytes, about 12.6 KB of the 16 KB before the runner's frames. If it's too tight, I'd patch the 9 KB array to the heap at build time, keeping the copy byte-identical.
- **Pin:** the frame hash isn't pinned yet (`0` in `kBaseline`). I'll pin after any speed or stack changes, so the hash isn't taken twice.
- **Bezel:** paddles and scores sit near the edges, so the round bezel clips the corners. An inscribed-square render would fix it but costs resolution, so it's your call after you've seen it.

**Request:** may I flash a Pong-pinned build (`-DSTART_HACK="pong" -DROTATE_SECONDS=0`) with a temporary stack high-water log, and capture about 150 s of serial? That gives fps, step, push, heap and stack. I'll send the output to a file and check "Hash of data verified". Serial port is `/dev/cu.usbmodem112401` unless you've moved the board.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/rod/build/stopwatch-screensaver/.claude/skills/device-run

# Flashing and measuring on the device

Moved verbatim from AGENTS.md.

- `pio run -e stopwatch`: build for the device. Add `-t upload` to flash.
  The device starts on a random hack; to pin one while examining it, prefix
  `PLATFORMIO_BUILD_FLAGS='-DSTART_HACK=\"galaxy\"'` (a name from `g_hacks[]`,
  any case; an unknown name falls back to random and logs it). Rebuild without
  it afterwards, since the define sticks to the build. Unescaped quotes fail
  with "error: 'truchet' was not declared in this scope".
  It rotates to the next hack every 90 s (a button press restarts the count);
  `-DROTATE_SECONDS=5` shortens that for leak testing and `=0` turns it off. A
  pinned build still rotates, so add `=0` to measure one hack.
  The log prints `rotate -> <hack> heap= psram=` at each change. Combine flags
  in one `PLATFORMIO_BUILD_FLAGS` string.
  `-DBADGE_NAME=\"Rod\ B.\"` sets the name badge text (default "Rod" over
  "Begbie"; `\n` starts a new line). Check a
  flag reached the binary with
  `strings -a -n 3 .pio/build/stopwatch/firmware.elf | grep -c '^Rod B\.$'`:
  plain `strings` skips anything under 4 characters.
  `-DQR_URL=\"https://example.com\"` sets the QR overlay's target (default the
  LinkedIn profile). Check it reached the binary with
  `strings -a .pio/build/stopwatch/firmware.elf | grep -c 'example.com'`.
  In a worktree session the harness refuses backslash-escaped flag values and
  `$(cat file)`. Use `PLATFORMIO_BUILD_FLAGS="'-DBADGE_NAME=\"Rod B.\"'
  '-DSTART_HACK=\"gears\"' -DROTATE_SECONDS=0"` with `.venv/bin/pio run -d
  firmware -e stopwatch -t upload` from the worktree root.
- Serial log: `.venv/bin/python -I tools/serial_capture.py <out-file>
  <seconds> [port]` reads `/dev/cu.usbmodem112401` at 115200 into a file and
  reopens the port when it goes away. Run it in the background with absolute
  paths, since background shells ignore `cd`. Lines to read:
  `run <hack> fps= step= push= sync= wait= rows=` (ms per frame in the hack,
  the push, the wait for the panel's TE edge before a synced push (only
  Unknown Pleasures; not counted in `push=`) and the wait; mean canvas rows
  sent per frame, 466 being a full push,
  though overlay redraws made while waiting can push it higher)
  and `switch -> <hack> press_waited=`. An empty capture, or "Device not
  configured", means the USB port went away and came back (a flash, a crash):
  reopen it in a loop. Opening the port resets the board
  (`rst:0x15 USB_UART_CHIP_RESET`, even with DTR/RTS held low): the overlay
  returns to nothing and a random hack starts. To measure one hack, flash a
  pinned build (`START_HACK` plus `ROTATE_SECONDS=0`), start the capture, then
  tap during it: the early windows are the baseline, the later ones have the
  overlay.
  `serial_capture.py` sets `dtr` and `rts` to False on an unopened
  `serial.Serial()` before `open()`, as any script of your own must: a reopen
  loop without that once parked the chip in its bootloader
  (`boot:0x3 ... waiting for download`, screen frozen). Recover, or reset just
  before a capture to log from boot (a hack's `fprintf(stderr)` reaches the
  log), with `.venv/bin/python .platformio/packages/tool-esptoolpy/esptool.py
  --chip esp32s3 --port /dev/cu.usbmodem112401 --after hard_reset read_mac`.
- Flash with `pio run -e stopwatch -t upload > file 2>&1`, never piped through
  `head`, and check for "Hash of data verified". The button steps backwards
  (Pyro, then Lightning, then Drift...). Work out how long a restart takes
  from the hack's cycle count times its frame time (Substrate: 10,000 cycles
  at about 160 ms is 27 minutes) and capture that long, with rotation off.
- `ad-flyingtoasters` force flags (add to `PLATFORMIO_BUILD_FLAGS`):
  `-DAD_TOASTERS_ART=0|1` (0 is 1-bit, 1 is colour) and
  `-DAD_TOASTERS_DONENESS=0|1|2` (light, medium, dark) and
  `-DAD_TOASTERS_SCALE=1|2` (2 is the default, with 6 flyers; 1 is the
  original size, with 10); a number outside those is an `#error`. It logs
  `ad-flyingtoasters: <art>, doneness=<level>` to stderr at start.
- To see where a GL hack's frame goes, add `-DGL_PROFILE`: a `glprof` line
  follows each `run` line with time per stage (clear, list, vertex, shade,
  tri, fill, point, line; nested, so vertex includes tri and fill). Time left
  over is the hack's own code. To compare builds, `.venv/bin/python -I
  tools/ab_flash.py --hack Gears --seconds 60 --rounds 2 --out <dir>
  "a=-DGL_PROFILE" "b=-DGL_PROFILE -DFOO"` builds each variant pinned, flashes
  them in turn and tabulates the windows. It flashes: run it only with Rod's
  go-ahead. It builds each hack's variants from the working tree when that
  hack's turn starts, so leave `src/` and `tools/tinygl_patch.py` alone until
  the last hack has built. It compares flag variants of one tree: to A/B a
  change, put it behind a temporary `-D` switch (as `-DPUSH_NO_DISC` does).
  It takes one `--hack` per run: loop several from a scratchpad script run
  with `run_in_background`, and `touch` a done file at the end.
- `-DDCACHE_LINE32` keeps the SDK's 32-byte data-cache lines for every hack
  (the default is 64 bytes, see `device-display.md`), so it is the A side of an
  `ab_flash` comparison. `-DPSRAM_BENCH` boots into `diag/psram_bench.h`
  instead of the runner and prints cost per cache miss, sequential rates and a
  working-set sweep; `-DPSRAM_BENCH_VARIANT=0..3` picks the line size and
  prefetch setting.
- `esptool` reads of the 16 MB flash need `--baud 921600` (about 3.5 minutes)
  and show no progress when piped.
- The port name changes with the USB socket the board is plugged into
  (`/dev/cu.usbmodem112401` became `/dev/cu.usbmodem101` on 2026-10-14). When
  it is missing, find the board without touching it:
  `ioreg -p IOUSB -l -w0 | grep -E "\+-o|idVendor|idProduct|USB Product
  Name|USB Serial Number"` lists USB devices, and
  `ioreg -r -c IOSerialBSDClient -l | grep IOCalloutDevice` lists the serial
  ports. The StopWatch is the "USB JTAG/serial debug unit" from Espressif
  (`idVendor` 12346, `idProduct` 4097). Its USB serial number is its MAC:
  Rod's board is `28:84:85:43:B2:70`, so check that before flashing a port
  you have not used before. Pass `--upload-port <port>` to `pio run -t upload`
  and read the same port for the serial log, and leave `platformio.ini`'s
  `upload_port` alone. Still ask Rod before each flash. The auto-mode
  classifier refused a flash to an overridden port once: give Rod the command
  to run with `!`.
- Another session may be using the board. Before flashing, run `lsof
  /dev/cu.usbmodem112401`: a "multiple access on port" upload error was
  another session's serial capture, and esptool's connect resets the board
  under it. Ask Rod before flashing over someone else's run.
- PlatformIO cleans the build directory, image and all, when
  `PLATFORMIO_BUILD_FLAGS` changes: an `-t nobuild -t upload` with other flags
  finds no `firmware.bin`. To keep several images, give each its own
  `PLATFORMIO_BUILD_DIR` (the build scripts all use `$BUILD_DIR`).
- Read `push=` from a hack's second 5 s window on: the name overlay is stamped
  inside the push timing while it shows, so the first window reads high.
- `heap=` and `psram=` are the reading at the end of a window, not a minimum:
  a hack with a long pause and nothing held in it (Celtic's 5 s `*delay2`)
  reads idle in every window. Sample while it works, or read `rotate ->`.
- Report a hack's lowest `fps=` window as well as its mean. HexTrail's step
  grows over a 65 s cycle: mean 15.3, worst window 10.8, and Rod saw an earlier
  build sag under 10 fps before the rotation moved on. Capture a full cycle and
  say which build the board holds when you stop.
- A boot is deterministic (same hack, layout and windows), so to compare two
  builds flash them alternately and compare window by window; one reading in
  three captures was an unexplained outlier, so never trust a single pair.
- Leak-testing with `-DROTATE_SECONDS=5`: internal heap falls about 26 KB
  during the first lap and then stays flat. Compare lap 2 with lap 3, not
  with lap 1. PSRAM should match exactly on every visit.
- To prove a device-only path the host cannot run (the ROM's `tinfl`), add a
  temporary `#ifdef` block after `printStats("boot")` in `main.cpp` that logs
  a checksum, compare it with one computed in Python, then `git checkout
  firmware/src/main.cpp` before pushing.

# Display, canvas and runner gotchas

Moved verbatim from the Gotchas section of AGENTS.md.

- M5GFX reads a plain `uint32_t` colour as RGB888. `TFT_RED` and friends are
  RGB565 constants. The canvas holds pixels already byte-swapped into the
  display's order (`rgb565()` returns them that way), and the display runs
  with `setSwapBytes(false)`. A swap done by M5GFX on each push cost 10 ms of
  every frame (#23: pushes of 41-45 ms became 31 ms). `px_swap()` turns a
  canvas pixel into ordinary RGB565 and back: only code that reads colour bits
  needs it (the logo loader, `dump_main.c`, tests). A hue-sweeping palette
  stays a rainbow with its bytes swapped (red, green and blue rotate), so only
  pure black and white, or a colour you know (Maze's red flame, its green
  solving path), expose a wrong order on the device. Host frames cannot,
  since the swap happens in the push; compare them with `px_swap` applied.
- A hack that takes colour bits out of pixel values itself (Substrate's alpha
  blend, in `point2rgb`) breaks on swapped pixels without a compile error and

    checked (a review reads the datasheet as calling `0x55` Auto Current Limit;

  24.8 ms, but a lone short write costs 1.3 us a miss. Pinned A/B, two

  pinned: a free-running lap changes random parameters per visit and showed
  false regressions of 3x on five hacks. A ROM prefetch setting (trigger 1,
  size 0) changed nothing; other settings are untried.

  the step contends for the cache). Many hacks are flagged, some of them GL
  (grep `repaints_all`, and `XLOCKMORE_HACK_REPAINTS_ALL`). The step slows by
  about 5 ms (both cores share the PSRAM cache), so the frame is roughly the
  step, not the longer of the two. Rules:

    test and the real-swap test in `test_push_overlap` run every flagged hack
    for 300 frames; 40 frames missed Halo, which the 300-frame run caught. GL
    hacks pass since #118 (see `gl.md`); GraphStat's swap run still fails.
  - Only a gain of 5% or more on a pinned A/B earns the flag. Deco and CCurve
    are paced by their own delays and gained 0 and 2.6%.

    byte-identical copy (Truchet, +25%) needs a wrapper to be flagged.

    while it shows, so the fps overlay reads the plain rate. Read `fps=` in
    the serial log for the overlapped one.

    second push (it blocked 25 ms), the overlay text canvas wraps one buffer
    and must follow `canvas.px`, and the newest-frame pointer must be dropped
    when a hack starts or Forest's first frame swapped the old picture back.

    pushes synchronously.

Contents of /Users/rod/build/stopwatch-screensaver/.claude/rules/device-display.md:

# Display, canvas and runner gotchas

Moved verbatim from the Gotchas section of AGENTS.md.

- M5GFX reads a plain `uint32_t` colour as RGB888. `TFT_RED` and friends are
  RGB565 constants. The canvas holds pixels already byte-swapped into the
  display's order (`rgb565()` returns them that way), and the display runs
  with `setSwapBytes(false)`. A swap done by M5GFX on each push cost 10 ms of
  every frame (#23: pushes of 41-45 ms became 31 ms). `px_swap()` turns a
  canvas pixel into ordinary RGB565 and back: only code that reads colour bits
  needs it (the logo loader, `dump_main.c`, tests). A hue-sweeping palette
  stays a rainbow with its bytes swapped (red, green and blue rotate), so only
  pure black and white, or a colour you know (Maze's red flame, its green
  solving path), expose a wrong order on the device. Host frames cannot,
  since the swap happens in the push; compare them with `px_swap` applied.
- A hack that takes colour bits out of pixel values itself (Substrate's alpha
  blend, in `point2rgb`) breaks on swapped pixels without a compile error and
  without a crash. `substrate_single.c` swaps at `XAllocColor` and
  `XSetForeground` so the hack sees ordinary RGB565; its golden-frame test
  fails if either is missing. Searching for `XGetPixel` finds none of this:
  dump every hack before and after a pixel-format change and `cmp` the frames.
  Pyro differs by a few hundred pixels, because it sorts projectiles by pixel
  value and so draws overlaps in another order.
- The display only gets the rows a hack drew. Every canvas write must go
  through `canvas_clear`, `canvas_point`, `hspan` or `canvas_paste_rect`
  (which record a span per row), or call `canvas_mark_dirty`, or the screen
  keeps the old pixels. The overlay text in `main.cpp` is the one deliberate
  bypass: it is written straight into `px`, marked by hand, and restored with
  `canvas_paste_rect`, which marks it again so the next push erases it.
  `test_push_present` replays every hack into a shadow display to catch a
  missed mark. M5GFX keeps a framebuffer for this panel and `endWrite` flushes
  one bounding box around everything written in a `startWrite` batch, so rows
  far apart must not share a batch (two corner pixels cost 11.7 ms together,
  0.1 ms apart). `push_plan` groups rows with a cost model fitted to device
  probes; its calibration shapes must include scattered rows, since compact
  rectangles cannot tell the models apart. Hacks that redraw unchanged pixels
  (CloudLife, Pedal) dirty nearly every row and gain little.
- The panel is round, so only the canvas's disc is pushed (issue #77).
  `canvas_set_disc` (in `main.cpp`) records each row's visible span: centre
  (w/2, h/2), and a pixel counts if any part of it is inside the circle.
  `push_plan` clips every dirty span to it and drops rows left empty. A hack
  with `sync_to_refresh` (Unknown Pleasures) still pushes whole rows, because
  its TE offset was swept for that push (#68). `-DPUSH_NO_DISC` turns off the
  push clip only, for an A/B: GL hacks still clear and fill only the disc
  (`gl.md`). Call `canvas_set_disc` before any `glshim_open`, which keeps a
  pointer to the spans. On the board: CloudLife's full frame 28.0 to 24.8 ms
  (26.2 to 28.4 fps), HexTrail 30.6 to 27.3 ms, Pyro 1.60 to 1.43 ms.
- Do not split a push into more batches than `push_plan`'s greedy grouping
  makes. Each extra flush in one push cost about 0.85 ms on the board, not the
  model's 17 us: a full disc frame in 19 bands took 39.9 ms against 24.7 ms in
  the greedy grouping's three, and per-row `pushImage` calls in one batch cost
  no more than one whole-image call (28.0 against 27.8 ms). The last flush of a
  push seems to finish while the hack draws its next frame; earlier ones are
  waited for. The cost model was fitted to single-flush pushes and cannot see
  this, so a split it rates cheaper can be slower.
- Hacks run on the Arduino `loopTask`, now set to a 16 KB stack in `main.cpp`.
  A hack with big local arrays can still overflow it (Rorschach's 9.6 KB did
  at 8 KB): the device reboots on that hack's first frame, and host tests
  cannot see it. Check the serial log for "Stack canary".
- `M5.update()` samples the buttons only when it runs and keeps no edge, so a
  press during a long hack step vanishes. `main.cpp` runs a 5 ms polling task
  on core 0 into `button_latch`, which needs the pin to hold a level for 30 ms.
  Reading the pin level inside a GPIO interrupt did not work: the release
  bounced and was counted as a second press. Check `press_waited` in the log.
- The runner caps a hack's delay at 10 s, and the loop credits only the push
  (31 ms; it was 41-45 ms between the byte-order fix and #23) against it,
  because a hack's delay is its pause after drawing. Compare device numbers
  with a baseline from the same build, not with old rows: Pyro fell from 30 to
  23 fps with no change to Pyro.
- `runner_start` paints the canvas in the hack's `background` resource before
  `init`, as `screenhack.c` paints the window, or black if it has none.
  Substrate is white; every other hack asks for black or nothing.
- Overlay modes cycle on a tap: nothing, name badge, QR code, fps, battery. The
  badge, the QR code and the info line share the stamp/unstamp path, and
  `kPatchMaxH` (140, or 248 with pixChicago) must cover the text block plus
  its outline: the badge is two lines, and `stampText` drops any line that
  would not fit. With `vendor/pixChicago.ttf` the badge is drawn in that font
  (`badge_font.py` rasterises it through `tools/make_badge_font.py` into an
  M5GFX `GFXfont`; the file is never committed, its licence being unclear) at
  x7. The font's grid is 8 px (9 px capitals, 3 px descenders, 13 px lines), so
  only whole scales look right, and `stampText`'s outline is `1 + scale / 4`
  px: 2 up to x7, 3 from x8, which is 24 then 48 stamps. Halftone pinned, badge
  on, push= in ms: Font8x8C64 x8 65.7; pixChicago x5 36.5, x6 39.2, x7 45.6,
  x8 82.7, x9 105.8 (no badge 0.10, since it overlaps the push). x7 is the
  largest scale before the cliff. `-DBADGE_SCALE=n` picks another. The
  battery is polled every 30 s (`M5.Power.getBatteryLevel()`; negative means a
  failed read, so the last good level stays). The QR code is encoded once at
  boot with M5GFX's `lgfx_qrcode` (`buildQr`, lowest version that holds
  `QR_URL`) into a 328 px white square, the biggest square inside the round
  screen. Each frame only copies it over the canvas and back (it reuses
  `infoPatch`, so that buffer is sized for the QR), and 328 rows are pushed
  every frame while it shows. The badge stamps 48 outline copies per frame and
  adds about 16 to 20 ms to `push=`. Read `wait=` as well as fps: a hack with
  delay slack (Galaxy) hides it, one running flat out (Squiral) does not.
- `lgfx_qrcode.h` (M5GFX's QR encoder, included at the top of `main.cpp`)
  defines `MODE_*`, `ECC_*` and `LOCK_VERSION`, which clash with other code, so
  `main.cpp` `#undef`s them straight after the include. Its init returns
  nonzero when the text is too long for a version; `buildQr` tries versions 1
  to 40 and, if none fits, leaves `qrPixels` null so the tap cycle skips QR.
- Overlay text (`main.cpp`) is stamped into the canvas, pushed, then the
  pixels under it are restored. Drawing on the display after `pushImage`
  flickered badly, because the next push erases it. The canvas must end each
  frame exactly as the hack left it.
- Tearing. The panel scans its memory 60 times a second and `pushImage` is not
  synchronised with it, so for a refresh the top of the screen shows one
  picture and the rest another. A thin line that moves a few pixels a frame can
  fall in the gap and vanish for a frame (Unknown Pleasures' flicker: a flat
  stretch of one line gone for about 17 ms). The panel's TE line is on GPIO 38
  (`OLED_TE`), M5GFX programs it (`0x35`, `0x44` at line 466) and nothing waits
  for it. It pulses every 16.82 ms for 1.1 ms. A full push is 20.6 ms copying
  into M5GFX's framebuffer plus 11.7 ms flushing to the panel (split by an
  outer `startWrite()` around the `pushImage`; the flush happens at the
  `endWrite`). `HackEntry::sync_to_refresh` (`XLOCKMORE_HACK_SYNCED`) starts
  the push `kTeSyncOffsetUs` after TE rises (`runner/te_sync.h`). Only
  Unknown Pleasures asks, because it costs up to a refresh of latency a frame.
- The offset (7.4 ms) is the middle of the clean window, found by a sweep:
  eight offsets across one refresh, 3 s each, the step number stamped on the
  screen, filmed at 120 fps. 3.2 to 9.5 ms had no vanished line in 39 updates;
  1.1 and 15.8 ms did, with the seam at film row 495 and film row 268: about 107
  film rows per millisecond (the camera frame is taller than the panel; the
  466-row panel scans about 28 rows per millisecond), so the bad window is only
  about 5 ms wide. It is valid for a full-frame push (the 20.6 ms copy). A push
  of another size moves the flush and the sweep would have to be repeated: the
  QR overlay's 328-row push is one, so a seam may show while the code is up.
  `-DTE_DIAG` logs the TE period and where pushes start.
- `te_sync.c` trusts few edges. Once it knows the period it accepts a rising
  edge only within period/16 of a whole number of periods since the last, so a
  missed edge or a stray pulse cannot move the lock; four misfits in a row drop
  the lock and relearn it. An edge further ahead than one period is stale (the
  32-bit microsecond counter can pass half its range with the line dead), and
  waiting stops 100 ms after the last edge. The ISR is placed in IRAM, but
  Arduino's pin dispatcher and `gpio_get_level` are in flash; that is safe only
  because `CONFIG_ARDUINO_ISR_IRAM` is unset. The run log's `sync=` is the wait
  for the edge and is left out of `push=`: compare `push=` across hacks, and add
  `sync=` to get the frame's latency.
- Reading a film of the display: iPhone slo-mo files store their first and
  last seconds at normal speed, so the label changes every ~100 frames there
  and every 360 in the 120 fps middle. Stabilise against the scenery (four
  corner patches; a mask edge around the display pins phase correlation at
  zero), level the rows, and count a vanish only when a line is missing across
  at least three 24 px windows on one row and not in a settled frame of the
  same update. A detector that finds nothing must also find the event you know
  is there: mine reported zero until a known vanish was used as a control, and
  reported many false events on steep line stretches until settled frames were.
- Every push also dims the screen, by an amount that grows with how far the
  picture scrolled since the last push (issue #68). Unknown Pleasures at
  upstream's speed: the dimmest of 12 bands falls to 0.86 of its settled value
  for about 25 ms (three camera frames at 120 fps) at each push, with or without
  TE sync. Rod sees it as pulsing. The dip by `*speed`, net of a noise floor
  taken inside the quiet part of each cycle:

  | Speed | Dip (points) | Rod |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | 0.2 | 1.0 | invisible, "really slow" |
  | 0.3 | 2.3 | invisible |
  | 0.4 | 4.0 | visible |
  | 0.5 | 5.6 | visible |
  | 1.0 | 14.5 | visible |

  - Shipped: `*speed: 0.3` in the registry override, about 0.75 px of scroll per
    push (derived from the hack's timing formula and the push rate, not
    measured). A faster push cannot reach the same step: 1.2 px at full speed
    needs about 10 Hz, and a push is 32 ms beside a 143 to 168 ms step. Rows,
    points and rate matter only through the step: 40 by 50 and 30 by 100 dip
    13 to 14% like the default. The 20-row sparse build (5.7% at about 1.56 px)
    sits about four points under the trend and is unexplained.
  - What it is not, each filmed: the write itself, bus or CPU load (a
    near-static scene pushes the same 466 rows at 5 Hz and does not dip), the
    push path (a copy of the canvas before each push still dips), a global
    dimming (stationary reference patches in the same frame stay steady while
    the strokes dip), and the picture's average level (on the host it changes
    under 1% from one pushed frame to the next in the default build, and more
    in the sparse one, which dips less). CABC was switched off with
    `0x55 = 0` and the dip stayed, but the panel's acceptance could not be
    checked (a review reads the datasheet as calling `0x55` Auto Current Limit;
    M5GFX's `readCommand` is a stub).
  - What it looks like: after a change a pixel takes frames to settle, and a
    rise is slower than a fall. Toggle patches, median over 14 events, 1.00 is
    settled, at the crossing and +1 to +3 frames: black to mid grey 0.69, 0.74,
    0.92, 0.98; mid grey to black 1.00 straight away; dark to mid grey 0.79,
    0.92, 0.93, 0.96. These are camera values, not calibrated luminance. The
    cause is not established: it is a transition-dependent loss, consistent
    with a local display response.
  - Overdrive did not help: newly lit pixels at 120% then the nominal frame gave
    a shallower dip with bright pulses before and after (peak to peak 9 to
    10%, against 8.8%) at a lower push rate. RGB565 clips the boost (an
    effective 1.146, and 7.9% of lit pixels have no headroom), so this is not
    a verdict on overdrive in general.
  - Measuring it: a noise-floor window must sit inside the quiet part of a
    cycle (a reference that runs into the next push's dip inflates the null),
    and a fold over integer periods shorter than its bins leaves empty bins.
    A shift probe must be counted on the host: 1 px sideways along near-
    horizontal lines relit only 20% of the lit pixels, 2 px vertically 94%.
    `dump_main.c` writes ordinary RGB565, so do not swap bytes again when
    reading its dumps. Do not let a reference patch reach the camera's ceiling
    (white read 252 to 255); mid grey read 212. Phone slo-mo files declare
    30 fps: the push period against the serial log's fps gave 120.
  - The probe builds (CABC off, a canvas copy with a vertical shift, reference
    and toggle patches, overdrive, row, point and speed overrides) were
    throwaway build flags on a branch that was not pushed; the comments on
    issue #68 describe each one.
- A hack's returned delay is waited after the push, and only the push counts
  against it, so its own step adds to the frame time: to hold a rate, return
  the target minus the step (`ad_flyingtoasters.c`: 19.5 fps became 28.9).
- PSRAM cost model (`diag/psram_bench.h`, `-DPSRAM_BENCH`): the data cache is
  32 KB, 8-way, 32-byte lines over 80 MHz octal PSRAM, and every miss costs
  about 0.92 us whatever the write size (sequential about 35 MB/s). Firmware
  switches to 64-byte lines (4-way) when a hack starts (`dcache.h`, through
  ROM calls the SDK header says an application should not make): sequential
  passes get about 28% faster and the full-frame push drops from 29 to
  24.8 ms, but a lone short write costs 1.3 us a miss. Pinned A/B, two
  rounds each: Deluxe, Interference, Kumppa, Abstractile +9%, HexTrail +17%,
  Marbling +7%, WhirlWindWarp +6%, Qix and Hexadrop +4%, Gears +3%; Lisa,
  Substrate, XRaySwarm, Pyro, RotZoomer flat. A `sync_to_refresh` hack
  keeps 32 bytes (Unknown Pleasures' offset was swept against the old copy
  time) and so does a hack with `dcache_line32` set in its `HackEntry`
  (Discrete: -5% fps, step 67.9 to 72.8 ms, many short spans). The other core
  is parked in IRAM with interrupts off while the cache is reconfigured
  (`dcache_with_other_core_parked`, over `esp_ipc_call`), as the SDK does for
  flash writes: `noInterrupts()` stops only the calling core.
  `-DDCACHE_LINE32` turns it off for every hack. Compare builds only
  pinned: a free-running lap changes random parameters per visit and showed
  false regressions of 3x on five hacks. A ROM prefetch setting (trigger 1,
  size 0) changed nothing; other settings are untried.
- A hack with `repaints_all` (`hack_entry.h`) draws its next frame while core 0
  pushes the last (`runner/push_overlap.[ch]`, issue #54): two canvases swap
  each frame, the worker pushes the finished one, and the loop credits that
  push's measured duration against the hack's delay. Pinned A/B on the board,
  plain to overlapped: Deluxe 14.0 to 19.0 fps, Compass 18.8 to 29.1, FuzzyFlakes
  18.4 to 28.9, Moire2 16.5 to 26.4, Scooter 22.1 to 28.4; Circuit 9.50 to 10.29,
  its step growing 17 ms (a miss-heavy line hack: the gain is smaller when
  the step contends for the cache). Many hacks are flagged, some of them GL
  (grep `repaints_all`, and `XLOCKMORE_HACK_REPAINTS_ALL`). The step slows by
  about 5 ms (both cores share the PSRAM cache), so the frame is roughly the
  step, not the longer of the two. Rules:
  - Flag a hack only if it never reads the canvas it starts from. The noise
    test and the real-swap test in `test_push_overlap` run every flagged hack
    for 300 frames; 40 frames missed Halo, which the 300-frame run caught. GL
    hacks pass since #118 (see `gl.md`); GraphStat's swap run still fails.
  - Only a gain of 5% or more on a pinned A/B earns the flag. Deco and CCurve
    are paced by their own delays and gained 0 and 2.6%.
  - A hack whose `HackEntry` comes from `XSCREENSAVER_MODULE` in the
    byte-identical copy (Truchet, +25%) needs a wrapper to be flagged.
  - Any overlay (name, badge, QR, fps, battery) makes the push synchronous
    while it shows, so the fps overlay reads the plain rate. Read `fps=` in
    the serial log for the overlapped one.
  - Three bugs the spike hit: a redraw from the wait loop must not dispatch a
    second push (it blocked 25 ms), the overlay text canvas wraps one buffer
    and must follow `canvas.px`, and the newest-frame pointer must be dropped
    when a hack starts or Forest's first frame swapped the old picture back.
  - `-DPUSH_NO_OVERLAP` turns it off for every hack (the A side of `ab_flash`).
    The spare canvas is 434 KB of PSRAM; if it will not allocate the firmware
    pushes synchronously.

Rod, Pong runs on the board but at 2.8 fps as copied. I'm stopping here to check the plan with you, because that's far below the 5–8 fps I guessed.

**What the board showed**
- **Speed:** 2.8 fps (2.6 in the first window), flat over 150 s. Step is 356 ms and push 24.8 ms, so the step is 93% of the frame.
- **Stability:** no canary, no reboot. Heap and PSRAM stayed flat.
- **Stack:** the high-water mark left 2,788 bytes free of 16 KB, so Pong uses about 13.6 KB. It's safe but with a thin margin. A heap patch for the 9 KB array stays an option if we keep it.
- **Flash:** 61.6% of the app partition.
- **State of the board and tree:** the board holds the pinned Pong build, with the temporary stack log inside it. I reverted that log in the tree (`git checkout main.cpp`). The WIP commit 789ec6b is unchanged.

**Why it's slow (my reasoning, not measured)**
- **Whole signal, every frame:** `analogtv` synthesises about 239,000 NTSC samples into a 955 KB float buffer in PSRAM, whatever Pong draws. It then filters 200 lines and renders 466 × 466 pixels.
- **Memory passes:** by my estimate that is about 150 ms of PSRAM passes (noise write, add, subtotals, read-back, image write, copy to canvas) on top of about 175 ms of float maths.
- **Wasted work:** nearly all of it repeats a picture that barely changes.

**Why it matters for Pong:** the game is paced per frame at about 30 fps upstream. At 2.8 fps the ball jumps about 6 px or more a frame, so it would look like slow motion with big jumps, not a game.

**Options**
1. **Split the step on the device.** I'd flash three temporary variants (skip the noise pass, skip the line loop, skip the put) through `ab_flash` to see which stage dominates before touching anything. About 15 minutes and three more flashes, which I'd need you to approve.
2. **Cut resolution and work.** Render the TV at the 266 × 200 minimum and scale up (`lowrez_put.h` style). A build-time patch could also limit the signal passes to the lines Pong draws. This risks the NTSC look and needs a byte-identity-preserving patch.
3. **Drop it.** Record it in `tools/failed_ports.txt` with the 2.8 fps number, as with Boing. It keeps the shim gaps, `analogtv`, and the `pong_tv.c` and notices work for the other analogtv hacks (xanalogtv, apple2, and others).

I'd go with option 1, since it costs little and tells us whether options 2 or 3 are realistic. Shall I do that?

"""Flash builds of the firmware in turn and compare their serial logs.

    .venv/bin/python -I tools/ab_flash.py --hack CubicGrid --seconds 60 \\
        --rounds 2 --out /tmp/ab base= iram=-DGL_IRAM "prof=-DGL_PROFILE -DGL_IRAM"

Each `name=flags` is a variant. Every variant is built once, pinned to the
hack with rotation off (`START_HACK`, `ROTATE_SECONDS=0`), and its image kept.
Then, round by round, each image is flashed and the serial log captured for
`--seconds`. A boot is deterministic, so alternating builds and comparing
window by window is how this repo measures a change (AGENTS.md).

This flashes the device: run it only with Rod's go-ahead. It never touches
the partition table or `ffat`; `pio run -t upload` writes what a normal
upload writes.
"""

import argparse
import os
import re
import statistics
import subprocess
import sys
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from pathlib import Path

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
FIRMWARE = ROOT / "firmware"

RUN = re.compile(r"^run (?P<hack>\S+) (?P<fields>.*)$")
GLPROF = re.compile(r"^glprof (?P<hack>\S+) (?P<fields>.*)$")
FIELD = re.compile(r"(\w+)=([-\d.]+)")


def parse_fields(text: str) -> dict[str, float]:
    """`fps=12.3 step=45.6ms rows=466` to {"fps": 12.3, "step": 45.6, ...}."""
    return {k: float(v) for k, v in FIELD.findall(text)}


@dataclass
class Capture:
    runs: list[dict[str, float]] = field(default_factory=list)
    glprof: list[dict[str, float]] = field(default_factory=list)


def parse_log(text: str, hack: str) -> Capture:
    """The `run` and `glprof` windows a log has for `hack` (any case)."""
    out = Capture()
    for raw in text.splitlines():
        line = raw.strip()
        for pattern, bucket in ((RUN, out.runs), (GLPROF, out.glprof)):
            m = pattern.match(line)
            if m and m.group("hack").lower() == hack.lower():
                bucket.append(parse_fields(m.group("fields")))
    return out


def summarise(windows: list[dict[str, float]], skip: int = 1) -> dict[str, float]:
    """Mean of each field, leaving out the first `skip` windows: the first
    holds the boot and, for push, the name overlay (AGENTS.md)."""
    kept = windows[skip:]

"""Makes BinaryRing's random scale a float literal.

`frand1()` is `random() << 1` times 4.65661287524579692411E-10, an exponent
literal, which tools/float_literals.py leaves as a double. Every particle calls
it twice a frame, so in the single-precision build each call would still be a
software double multiply on the board. The copied binaryring.c stays
byte-identical; firmware/patch_float_literals.py runs this on its text.
"""

OLD = "4.65661287524579692411E-10)"
NEW = "4.65661287524579692411E-10f)"


def float_random_scale(source: str) -> str:
    found = source.count(OLD)
    if found != 1:
        raise ValueError(
            f"expected 1 of `{OLD}` in binaryring.c, found {found}; has upstream changed?"
        )
    return source.replace(OLD, NEW)

"""Makes BinaryRing's random scale a float literal.

`frand1()` is `random() << 1` times 4.65661287524579692411E-10, an exponent
literal, which tools/float_literals.py leaves as a double. Every particle calls
it twice a frame, so in the single-precision build each call would still be a
software double multiply on the board. The copied binaryring.c stays
byte-identical; firmware/patch_float_literals.py runs this on its text.
"""

OLD = "4.65661287524579692411E-10)"
NEW = "4.65661287524579692411E-10f)"


def float_random_scale(source: str) -> str:
    found = source.count(OLD)
    if found != 1:
        raise ValueError(
            f"expected 1 of `{OLD}` in binaryring.c, found {found}; has upstream changed?"
        )
    return source.replace(OLD, NEW)

# Scorer and speed-prediction gotchas

Moved verbatim from the Gotchas section of AGENTS.md.

- `score_hacks.py` rates effort by call sites, not loop trips: Flame (all
  `double` maths) is rated S but runs at 2-7 fps, and Braid was rated S and
  runs at 3-9 fps. The Speed column runs the hack on the host instead and ranks
  the device step well (Spearman about 0.9 over the 29 hacks it was fitted to,
  and four more ported since fell where predicted), but a low band does not
  clear a hack that does software `double` maths: the device ran 60-1,500
  times the host time, most for the double-bound ones. It says nothing about
  memory: Celtic as copied held about 300 KB of the 325 KB of free heap and
  ran at 1.2 fps (it is registered again after issue #37, see `hacks.md`). A
  failed port that has its source and a measured row (Hypnowheel, Boing)
  still counts in `speed_backtest.py`, probed standalone. Measure on the
  device, and read
  `docs/speed-backtest.md` before trusting a band. A hack with gaps (M and
  above) cannot be built, so it has no Speed.
- A `failed_ports.txt` name is the scorer's: the source file's stem
  (`companion` for Companion Cube), as the assessment's rows spell it. Check
  the cross appears after regenerating.
- `score_hacks.py --no-probe` also blanks the Speed column of the generated
  assessment ("high (2 ms)" becomes "-"): commit the output of a full run. The
  backtest reads a measured row only when its name is the bare hack name
  (`| Deluxe |`); a row with a note in brackets is skipped, so put the build
  that is registered in the bare row.
- `score_hacks.py` counts a hack as ported if `&<name>_hack` appears anywhere
  in the text of `g_hacks[]`, `#ifdef` or not, and then refuses one that
  `failed_ports.txt` also lists. A probe-only entry (Hypnowheel's
  `HYPNOWHEEL_PROBE`) goes through a macro defined above the array.
- `speed_backtest.py` probes a dropped (shelved) hack standalone. A GL one
  (its source has `USE_GL`: Hypnowheel) is built with the GL layer through
  `gl_budget.measure`, which also converts the `images/gen/<n>_png.h` textures
  it includes. One that still cannot be built (BlockTube needs `glFogi`, which
  the GL layer lacks) is left out with a `note:` on stderr, so read the run's
  output for notes. The scorer also lists calls inside code that is never
  compiled (`XCreateBitmapFromData` in Cynosure's `DO_STIPPLE` block) as gaps.
- `score_hacks.py` skips the names in `OWN_HACKS` (our own hacks with no
  xscreensaver source, now `ad_flyingtoasters`) and still reports any other
  registry name it cannot scan as a typo. `speed_backtest.py` runs on the host
  only the registered hacks that have a device-measured row, so a `dump` build
  without the After Dark disk (which lacks the toasters) still works.
- `probe_hacks.MEASURED_ROW` takes only a number range in the fps cell: a
  row like `| HexTrail | 10.8-50.6, mean 15.3 |` is skipped, so the assessment
  shows `-` for its step and the backtest leaves it out. Put the mean in the
  prose.
- A call to an undeclared shim function also shows up as a gap named
  `error: incompatible integer to pointer conversion ...` (the implicit `int`
  return). It is noise beside the real gap (Barcode's `utf8_to_latin1`), but it
  counts towards the band.
